thread.title: Rep. Brownlee presents Medicaid Savings Act to address administrative waste in Ohio system
thread.title_full: Rep. Brownlee presents Medicaid Savings Act to address administrative waste in Ohio system

author: Buckeye Reporter
title: Rep. Brownlee presents Medicaid Savings Act to address administrative waste in Ohio system
text:
State Representative Karen Brownlee of Symmes Township provided sponsor testimony on May 22 for House Bill 780, known as the Medicaid Savings Act, which aims to reduce administrative waste within Ohio’s Medicaid system and focus resources on healthcare for residents.
Brownlee said that while there have been recent allegations of fraud and abuse, much of the waste in the Medicaid program is due to administrative redundancies across seven managed care organizations operating in Ohio. She said, “The Medicaid Savings Act is a proven way to reduce waste across the Medicaid system, and it is estimated to save Ohio $1B over a two-year period. The circus of unproven fraud by Medicaid patients and providers only serves to destabilize Ohio’s healthcare system.”
The proposed legislation would shift administration from the current Managed Care Organization model to an Administrative Services Organization model. This new structure would consolidate care management for medical, behavioral health, and nursing services into a single line of administration. Supporters say this could simplify management processes, lower costs, and improve access to care.
Dr. Phil Lichtenstein, former Medical Director at Best Point Behavioral Health, said, “This bill promises to eliminate up to $850 million per year of wasteful spending in the administration of Medicaid so that these taxpayer dollars can be used, instead, to strengthen and expand direct clinical services for Ohio’s 3 million Medicaid recipients. Rather than raising taxes, the bill allows us to get more bang for the bucks we’re already spending.” Dee Chavez, RN and regional coordinator with Healthcare for All Ohioans, added: “As a nurse, I see how people struggle to get care… This bill would increase provider and hospital payments to equitable levels, increase access…and could keep our rural hospitals open.”
The legislation is modeled after similar reforms implemented in Connecticut as well as changes made through Ohio’s single payer Pharmacy Benefit Manager programs. According to supporters cited in testimony at the hearing process referenced by Brownlee’s office,
the singular ASO model has improved data collection on patient outcomes while reducing costs.
Senators Louis Blessing (Colerain Township) and Beth Liston (Dublin) have introduced an identical companion measure—Senate Bill 386—in the Senate.

This new structure would consolidate care management for medical, behavioral health, and nursing services into a single line of administration.
